summary: IKEv2 is part of IPsec and sets up the security associations. This informational RFC describes a minimal initiator-only version for constrained nodes, leaving out optional features those devices do not need so the implementation stays small.

plainLanguage.summary: IKEv2 is the part of IPsec that checks who the other end is and sets up the keys that protect the data. Full IKEv2 is too big for tiny devices. This document describes a cut-down initiator that makes two exchanges, uses a pre-shared secret instead of certificates, and refuses everything else, while still working with a full IKEv2 server.

questions: what is a minimal ikev2 implementation
can two minimal ikev2 initiators talk to each other
which ikev2 exchanges does a minimal initiator use
what is a minimal ikev2 initiator
subtitle: The smallest IKEv2 initiator that still talks to a full server, for devices with little memory and power.

tldr.problem: The Internet Protocol Suite is increasingly used on small devices with severe limits on power, memory and processing, and a full IKEv2 implementation is too large for them.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes an initiator that supports only the IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH exchanges, uses shared secret authentication, and answers every other request with an empty or error reply.
tldr.outcome: The result is a standalone specification for a small initiator that interoperates with a full IKEv2 responder, although two minimal initiators cannot talk to each other.

today: RFC 7815 is an Informational document published in March 2016. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it states that it does not update or modify RFC 7296, which remains the authoritative description of the protocol if the two ever conflict.

sections.title: What a Minimal Initiator Leaves Out
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol Suite is increasingly used on small devices with severe constraints on power, memory and processing resources. This document describes a minimal IKEv2 implementation for such constrained nodes that is interoperable with RFC 7296. IKEv2 is a component of IPsec used for performing mutual authentication and for establishing and maintaining Security Associations (SAs).

A minimal IKEv2 implementation supports only the initiator end of the protocol. It supports only the initial IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH exchanges and does not initiate any other exchange. It replies with an empty or error message to all incoming requests.

That leaves most optional features of IKEv2 out: NAT traversal, IKE SA rekey, Child SA rekey, multiple Child SAs, deleting Child or IKE SAs, Configuration payloads, Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) authentication and COOKIEs. The document is intended to be standalone, with everything needed to implement IKEv2 copied into it except the description of the cryptographic algorithms.

The main use case is machine-to-machine communication, where the node that opens the connection is very small and the other end is a larger device. The document gives a remote garage door opener and a room temperature sensor as examples. Those devices sleep for a long time and wake up periodically, and the data transfer is always started by the small node. While the device sleeps it does not maintain the IKEv2 SA, so it creates the SA again each time it wakes up, and no liveness checks for the server are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A minimal initiator does one job: it starts connections and sets up the keys that protect them. It never starts anything else, and it answers anything it does not understand with an empty or error reply. That keeps the code small enough for a device with little memory or power.

sections.title: The Exchanges a Minimal Initiator Uses
sections.content:
All IKEv2 communication consists of pairs of messages, a request and a response, called an exchange. Every request requires a response. For every pair of messages the initiator is responsible for retransmission after a timeout, the retransmission MUST be bitwise identical to the original request, and the retransmission times MUST increase exponentially. The responder MUST never retransmit a response unless it receives a retransmission of the request.

IKEv2 runs over UDP port 500, and all implementations MUST be able to send, receive and process IKEv2 messages up to 1280 octets long. An implementation MUST accept incoming requests even if the source port is not 500, and MUST respond to the address and port from which the request was received.

The minimal implementation uses only the first two exchanges. IKE_SA_INIT carries the SAi1 payload, which states the cryptographic algorithms the initiator supports for the IKE SA, the KEi and KEr payloads with Diffie-Hellman values, and the Ni and Nr nonces. The response carries SAr1 with the chosen cryptographic suite, KEr, Nr and possibly a CERTREQ payload, which a shared-secret implementation ignores. A minimal implementation most likely supports exactly one set of cryptographic algorithms, so its SAi1 payload is static, and it only has to check that the SAr1 it receives matches the proposal it sent.

IKE_AUTH then carries the identity and the proof of the shared secret, the second SA proposal for the Child SA, and the Traffic Selectors that say which traffic the Child SA covers. The responder replies with the accepted offer and the selected Traffic Selectors, which may be a subset of what the initiator proposed. In the minimal implementation both SA payloads and both TS payloads are mostly static; the initiator's TS payloads will most likely be full wildcard ranges or a single pair of IP addresses, and using a single address pair is simpler because the responder then either accepts it or returns an error.

Beyond these two exchanges the minimal implementation has to understand a CREATE_CHILD_SA request enough to send back a NO_ADDITIONAL_SAS error, and an INFORMATIONAL request enough to send back an empty INFORMATIONAL response. If such a request carries an unsupported critical payload, the implementation MUST ignore it and reply with the UNSUPPORTED_CRITICAL_PAYLOAD notification, whose data holds the one-octet payload type.
sections.plainLanguage: The device sends two exchanges and stops. The first agrees on encryption algorithms and exchanges the values used to make a shared secret. The second proves the device knows its pre-shared secret and says which traffic the new keys should cover. Any other request is answered with an error or an empty reply.

sections.title: Proving Identity With a Shared Secret
sections.content:
With shared secret authentication the peers are authenticated by each calculating a Message Authentication Code (MAC) over a block of data. The initiator computes AUTH = prf(prf(Shared Secret, "Key Pad for IKEv2"), InitiatorSignedOctets) and the responder computes the same formula over its own signed octets. The string Key Pad for IKEv2 is 17 ASCII characters without null termination. An implementation can precalculate the inner prf and store only its output, which is possible because a minimal implementation usually supports only one PRF.

The initiator signs the first message, the IKE_SA_INIT request, starting with the first octet of the first SPI in the header and ending with the last octet of the last payload in that message. Appended to this, for the purpose of computing the signature, are the responder's nonce Nr and the value prf(SK_pi, IDi'). The responder's signed octets start at the first octet of the first SPI in the header of the IKE_SA_INIT response and end with the last octet of the last payload in that response, with the initiator's nonce Ni and the value prf(SK_pr, IDr') appended. All payloads inside the message are covered, including any payload types the document does not list, and neither the nonces nor the values prf(SK_pr, IDr') and prf(SK_pi, IDi') are transmitted.

Because a minimal implementation usually has only one host to connect to, it has only one shared secret and does not need to pay much attention to the IDr payload. If the other end sends an AUTH payload that the initiator can verify with the shared secret it holds, then the initiator knows the other end is the peer it was configured to talk to.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side proves it knows the shared secret by computing a code over the first message and sending that code. The code covers the whole message plus the other side's random value, so it cannot be reused for a different conversation.

sections.title: Deriving the Keys
sections.content:
After the IKE_SA_INIT exchange each party can generate SKEYSEED, from which all keys for that IKE SA are derived. The seed is SKEYSEED = prf(Ni | Nr, g^ir), where g^ir is the shared secret from the ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange, represented as a string of octets in big endian order and padded with zeros to the length of the modulus. The seven keys are then taken in order from the output of a stretched pseudorandom function: prf+(SKEYSEED, Ni | Nr | SPIi | SPIr).

SK_d is used for deriving new keys for the Child SAs. SK_ai and SK_ar are the keys for the integrity protection algorithm that authenticates the component messages of later exchanges. SK_ei and SK_er encrypt and decrypt all subsequent exchanges. SK_pi and SK_pr are used when generating an AUTH payload. The lengths of SK_d, SK_pi and SK_pr MUST be the preferred key length of the pseudorandom function that was agreed on. A separate SK_e and SK_a is computed for each direction, so the keys protecting messages from the original initiator are SK_ai and SK_ei.

The keying material for the Child SA created by the IKE_AUTH exchange is generated as KEYMAT = prf+(SK_d, Ni | Nr), using the nonces from the IKE_SA_INIT exchange. A single Child SA negotiation may result in several Security Associations, because ESP and Authentication Header SAs exist in pairs, one in each direction. All keys for SAs carrying data from the initiator to the responder are taken before those going the other way. For ESP and AH, the encryption key, if any, MUST be taken from the first bits of the keying material and the integrity key, if any, from the remaining bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides combine their random values with the Diffie-Hellman result to get one seed, and they stretch that seed into the keys they need. Separate keys are used for each direction, for encryption and for integrity, and the child connection's keys come from a further stretch of one of them.

sections.title: Conformance Requirements
sections.content:
For an implementation to be called conforming to the RFC 7296 specification, it MUST be possible to configure it to accept Public Key Infrastructure using X.509 certificates containing and signed by RSA keys of size 1024 or 2048 bits, where the identity passed is any of ID_KEY_ID, ID_FQDN, ID_RFC822_ADDR or ID_DER_ASN1_DN. It MUST also be possible to configure it to accept shared key authentication where the identity passed is any of ID_KEY_ID, ID_FQDN or ID_RFC822_ADDR, and to accept a responder authenticated with X.509 certificates while the initiator uses shared key authentication.

This document supports only the second of those cases and does not support X.509 certificates at all. Certificates are left out because they would add a lot of complexity: the actual code changes in the IKEv2 protocol are small, but the certificate validation code would be more complex than the whole minimal implementation itself. Because full RFC 7296 responders must also support shared key authentication, a minimal implementation can interoperate with every implementation that is compliant with RFC 7296.

Where public-key authentication is needed for scalability, the document points to raw public keys as the best compromise, described in Appendix B.2.
sections.plainLanguage: To be called conformant, an implementation has to be able to accept certificates, even though this minimal one never sends them. Accepting shared secrets is enough in practice, because every full server has to support shared secrets as well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document states that it implements the same protocol as RFC 7296, so all security considerations from that specification apply here as well. It does not add any of its own.

Two implementation notes from the document's own text are worth keeping in mind. A minimal implementation using shared secrets will ignore the CERTREQ payload in the IKE_SA_INIT response, and the shared secret is the only thing standing between the device and an impersonation attempt. Appendix B.2 makes the point directly: in some scenarios shared secret authentication is not safe enough, because anybody who knows the secret can impersonate the server, and if the secret is printed on the side of the device then anybody with physical access can read it.
sections.plainLanguage: All the security rules of the full IKEv2 specification apply, because this is the same protocol with fewer options. The document adds no rules of its own. One thing it does point out is that a pre-shared secret printed on a device can be read by anyone who picks the device up.

items.title: Initiator only
items.text: It supports only the initiator end of the protocol and never starts an exchange the responder did not ask for.

items.title: Two exchanges
items.text: It sends IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH and nothing else.

items.title: Everything else is refused
items.text: Incoming requests get an empty or error reply, such as NO_ADDITIONAL_SAS for CREATE_CHILD_SA.

items.title: Shared secret only
items.text: It authenticates with a pre-shared secret and does not support X.509 certificates.

fields.name: Initiator's SPI
fields.desc: Chosen by the initiator to identify a unique IKE security association. It must not be zero.

fields.name: Responder's SPI
fields.desc: Chosen by the responder. It must be zero in the first message of an initial exchange.

fields.name: Next Payload
fields.desc: Type of the payload that immediately follows the header.

fields.name: Major Version
fields.desc: Must be set to 2, and messages with a higher major version are dropped.

fields.name: Minor Version
fields.desc: Must be set to zero when sending and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Exchange Type
fields.desc: 34 for IKE_SA_INIT, 35 for IKE_AUTH, 36 for CREATE_CHILD_SA, 37 for INFORMATIONAL.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Options carried in bits, including Response, Version and Initiator.

fields.name: Message ID
fields.desc: Matches a request to its response and identifies retransmissions.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the whole IKE message.

messages.label: IKE_SA_INIT request
messages.note: SAi1 with the algorithms, KEi with the Diffie-Hellman value, and the nonce Ni.

messages.label: IKE_SA_INIT response
messages.note: SAr1 with the chosen suite, KEr, Nr, and possibly CERTREQ, which is ignored.

messages.label: IKE_AUTH request
messages.note: SK{IDi, AUTH, SAi2, TSi, TSr, N(INITIAL_CONTACT)}.
